job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior financial analyst at Tidewell Power, a small wind and solar company in Glasgow. I started in August. Mornings I update the cost models for new projects, and afternoons I'm in calls with engineers who tell me their numbers are 'roughly right'. I share a tenement flat with my cousin Ines and a guy who's always on a climbing wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I can sit with a messy model and make it clearer, and I use AI for half of that, like writing the script that pulls the grid prices in each morning. What wears me down is meetings where nobody decides anything. My parents are both teachers and they've said they'll cover me if the startup wobbles, which makes me bolder than I'd otherwise be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, then the tools I use are good enough and we can all stop talking about a revolution. At work I'd say it's a decent calculator for words. Online I'd probably post a neat trick for cleaning spreadsheets, since I enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my edge stays small, because everyone gets the same tools. But I'm good at the actual job too, and Tidewell is growing, so I'd be fine. There are loads of energy and finance jobs in Glasgow, and my savings cover more than six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, learn more of the energy-market side, and sit my first professional exam in the spring. I'd keep automating my own reports, because it gets me home an hour earlier. And I'd save around 30 percent, then maybe put some into a global index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored, to be honest, because the exciting version would at least be interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would change for you if it fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Without AI I'd write the grid-price script slowly, probably in two days instead of one, and I'd lean on the senior analyst Craig more. My daily time would slip. The tools just make me a bit quicker, so I'd lose some speed, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the startup itself. If Tidewell loses a big contract, the first people to go are the newest, and that's me. But I'd say that's an ordinary risk of working at a small firm, not an AI thing. I'd bounce back, because I've got savings and my parents.

say: I'd say the tools are a **decent calculator** for words and nothing more.
I'd post a neat trick for **cleaning spreadsheets**, because I enjoy it.
think: I think my **edge** stays small, because everyone gets the same tools.
Tidewell is **growing**, and Glasgow has lots of energy and finance jobs.
do: Sit my first professional **exam** in the spring.
Keep **automating** my own reports to get home an hour earlier.
Save around **30 percent** and start a global index fund.
feel: I feel **calm**, maybe a little bored without the exciting version.
S0.quote: If Tidewell loses a big contract, the first people to go are the newest, and that's me.
fieldNote: Freya is **secure** and adaptable, so a no-change world suits her.
She separates **startup risk** from AI risk, which is sensible for her situation.
Daily AI use already **saves** her an hour, a real baseline.

steps.text: Sit my first professional exam this spring
Automate my weekly cost reports with scripts
Save 30 percent of pay each month
Start a monthly global index fund contribution

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving fast and the people who learn the tools will do well, but that's not a reason to leave anyone behind. I'd say firms and government have to pay for training, not leave people to find it on YouTube at night. And I'd post about it, because I like sharing what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior analyst role changes shape. The model-building I do now, a tool will do in minutes, and Tidewell will hire fewer analysts. But I'm the one writing the scripts, so I'm in the group that makes the team smaller rather than the group that disappears. That's a slightly odd place to be, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push deeper into the energy side, so my value isn't just the spreadsheets. I'd take a short course in data engineering at night, about a hundred pounds, and try to build a tool the team actually uses. I'd also bank more, since a few more months of cushion means I can say no to a bad role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy, both at once. I like that I'm ahead of most of my course, but I know being ahead is no guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see your own role changing at Tidewell in two or three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd become half analyst, half builder. Craig would give me the judgement calls and I'd do the tooling for the team. That means the job exists, but looks nothing like what I was hired for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to graduates who don't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pick one tool and go deep for a month, not ten tools for a day each. I'd run a lunch session at Tidewell and put the notes on our wiki. I'd also tell them not to be ashamed to ask; I didn't know any of this either until I tried.

say: I'd say learning the tools helps, but firms must **pay for training**.
I'd post what I learn, because sharing is how I **stay ahead**.
think: Privately, I think the **junior analyst** role changes shape and Tidewell hires fewer.
I'm writing the scripts, so I'm in the group that **shrinks** the team.

Take a night course in **data engineering**, about £100.
Build a **tool** the team actually uses.
feel: I feel **excited** and a bit uneasy, because being ahead is no guarantee.
S1.quote: Pick one tool and go deep for a month, not ten tools for a day each.
fieldNote: Freya sees herself on the **builder** side, a hedge against her own role shrinking.
She is honest that being ahead is **no guarantee**.
She turns learning into **sharing**, which builds her standing at work.

steps.text: Take a night course in data engineering
Build a reporting tool the Tidewell team uses
Run a lunch session on AI tools for colleagues
Bank an extra £200 a month for a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now, and honestly I think most of them won't be ready. I'd push for a basic income and a public stake in AI, because it can't all go to a few firms. I'd also say it online in as plain terms as I could, because people need to hear a real person say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone within a couple of years of AGI, full stop. A junior financial analyst does thinking work by definition. I'd be twenty-four and starting again with a head start in the tools, but so would everyone else. The robots come three years later, but I've never done anything hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd check what I can afford, which is more than six months, and tighten up a little. I'd save 60 percent of my pay while it lasts. Then I'd look for anything that needs a person in the room, like energy-site visits, and try to get a seat on whatever project builds the next wind farm. And I'd tell my parents plainly what I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also strangely awake. I'd be watching a wave come in and trying to decide whether to run or surf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. What would you do in the first month after you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't move in with them straight away, because I'd lose my independence and the jobs are in Glasgow. But I'd lean on them for money, and I'd say yes if they offered. That's what the safety net is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide about moving in with family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest, there are only two years, so I wouldn't spend on exams that finish after the deadline. I'd cancel the professional exam fees and use the time for work that builds me into whatever's next. That includes volunteering with a local energy co-op, so I'm in a network people trust.

say: I'd say governments must act now and push for a **basic income**.
I'd insist on a **public stake** in AI, so it doesn't all go to a few firms.
think: Privately, I think my **job** is gone within a couple of years of AGI.
Hands-on robots come later, but I've never done anything **hands-on**.
do: Check what I can afford and save **60 percent** of pay.
Cancel the **exam fees** that finish after the deadline.
Join a local **energy co-op** to build a trusted network.
feel: I feel **scared** but strangely awake, like deciding whether to run or surf.
S2.quote: I'd be watching a wave come in and trying to decide whether to run or surf.
fieldNote: Freya's **adaptability** lets her plan rather than freeze, even though she expects to lose the job.
She is willing to use **family** money without guilt.
She drops long-term **exams** because their timing no longer fits.

steps.text: Save 60 percent of my pay while the job lasts
Cancel the professional exam fees
Campaign for a basic income and a public AI stake
Join a local energy co-op for a network

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to build a fair system, so let's not waste it on arguing. I'd push for paid retraining and a tax on the firms that gain most. I'd say it in a way that doesn't scare people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: it's the end of the junior analyst route as I know it, but I'd have a few years to get somewhere higher. Five years is enough to be a senior analyst or to build something of my own. By 2031 I'll be twenty-seven. I'd probably still have a job but I'd be ready to leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my professional qualification only if it helps me within two years, otherwise skip it. I'd use my AI skills to start a small consultancy for community energy groups at weekends, maybe six hours a week. And I'd put a lot into index funds and a bit into the co-op, so I own a piece of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. If I picture it right, five years is like a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is longer. What would you try that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, finish the data course and try three clients. Year two, if it works, go part time at Tidewell. Year three, decide whether to run it full time. By year five I'd either be running a tiny business or working for someone who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your own timeline look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller scale. In two years I'm cutting back and clinging on. In five I'm building a small thing, and I can afford to fail twice because I've got my parents and my savings.

say: I'd say we have time to build a **fair system** and should not waste it arguing.
I'd push for **paid retraining** and a tax on firms that gain most.
think: I think the junior analyst **route** ends, but five years gets me somewhere higher.
By 2031 I'll be twenty-seven, ready to **leave** a job I still have.
do: Start a small **consultancy** for community energy groups at weekends.
Put money into **index funds** and a little into the co-op.
Go part time at Tidewell if the **clients** come in.
feel: I feel **excited**, because five years is like a runway.
S3.quote: I can afford to fail twice because I've got my parents and my savings.
fieldNote: Freya treats five years as a **runway** for a side business, a very adaptable response.
The plan is staged, with decision points in each **year**.

steps.text: Find three community energy clients for weekend consulting
Put savings into index funds and a local energy co-op
Finish the data engineering course this year
Go part time at Tidewell once the clients pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, so let's not pretend we're surprised. I'd say schools should teach people how to work with AI from the first year, and that the benefits should be shared in shorter work weeks. I'd say it a bit cheerfully, because I really do think it can go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable to me. By 2036 I'll be thirty-two, with a decade of experience in a field that's changed three times. I think I'd be fine, but I'd always be watching for the next shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Tidewell and learn the energy market properly. I'd save for a flat in Glasgow, maybe by twenty-six, and keep a side project going. I'd also join a policy group on AI and work, because I'd like to help get this right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm and a bit curious. I'm someone who likes a challenge, as long as I'm not being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What kind of life do you picture by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I imagine a flat with a view of the river, a small business, and a partner who's also doing something unusual. I'd probably work four days a week. And I'd be teaching younger people how to use the tools, because I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would you give someone just graduating now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools early, but don't think the tools are the job. Be someone people want to hire because you ask good questions, and keep a cushion so you can say no. I wish I'd known that the people who thrive are the ones who stay curious.

say: I'd say a decade is plenty, so let's **teach** AI skills from the first year of school.
I'd argue the gains should be shared as **shorter work weeks**.
think: Ten years feels **manageable**, and I'd be thirty-two with a decade of experience.
I'd always be watching for the **next shift**, but I'm not afraid.
do: Keep working at Tidewell and learn the **energy market** properly.
Save for a **flat** in Glasgow by age twenty-six.
Join a **policy group** on AI and work.
feel: I feel **mostly calm** and curious, as long as I'm not rushed.
S4.quote: Learn the tools early, but don't think the tools are the job.
fieldNote: Freya is **optimistic** in the long scenario, a natural fit for her curious style.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's not that I'd have no ideas, it's that I'd have no time for them to pay off. What would help is a basic income that starts before things break, paid retraining, and firms being open about their plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I know I'm in a privileged spot. I have a degree, a job, parents who'd catch me, and I use these tools every day. I'm not worried about me, but about people who don't have what I have.

headlineQuote: I'm not worried about me, but about people who don't have what I have.
portrait: Freya, 22, is a **junior financial analyst** at a small wind and solar company in Glasgow, and uses AI tools every day.
Her parents are teachers who would **catch her**, which makes her bold about risk.
She sees herself as a builder who makes her own role smaller, and she plans **side income** and consulting.
Her mood is calm in most scenarios, with **anxiety** only when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because she would have no time for her ideas to pay off.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** that starts before things break, plus paid retraining.
